{{Short description|Family of sets closed under countable unions}}
In [[mathematics]], a nonempty collection of [[Set (mathematics)|sets]] is called a '''{{sigma}}-ring''' (pronounced ''sigma-ring'') if it is [[Closure (mathematics)|closed]] under countable [[Union (set theory)|union]] and [[Complement (set theory)|relative complementation]].

== Formal definition ==

Let <math>\mathcal{R}</math> be a nonempty [[Family of sets|collection of sets]]. Then <math>\mathcal{R}</math> is a '''{{sigma}}-ring''' if:
# Closed under countable [[Union (set theory)|unions]]: <math>\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} A_{n} \in \mathcal{R}</math> if <math>A_{n} \in \mathcal{R}</math> for all <math>n \in \N</math>
# Closed under [[Complement (set theory)|relative complementation]]: <math>A \setminus B \in \mathcal{R}</math> if <math>A, B \in \mathcal{R}</math>

== Properties ==

These two properties imply:
<math display="block">\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} A_n \in \mathcal{R}</math>
whenever <math>A_1, A_2, \ldots</math> are elements of <math>\mathcal{R}.</math> 

This is because
<math display="block">\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty A_n = A_1 \setminus \bigcup_{n=2}^{\infty}\left(A_1 \setminus A_n\right).</math>

Every {{sigma}}-ring is a [[Delta-ring|δ-ring]] but there exist δ-rings that are not {{sigma}}-rings.

== Similar concepts ==

If the first property is weakened to closure under finite union (that is, <math>A \cup B \in \mathcal{R}</math> whenever <math>A, B \in \mathcal{R}</math>) but not countable union, then <math>\mathcal{R}</math> is a [[Ring of sets|ring]] but not a {{sigma}}-ring.

== Uses ==

{{sigma}}-rings can be used instead of [[Sigma-algebra|{{sigma}}-fields]] ({{sigma}}-algebras) in the development of [[Measure (mathematics)|measure]] and [[Integral|integration]] theory, if one does not wish to require that the [[Universe (mathematics)|universal set]] be measurable. Every {{sigma}}-field is also a {{sigma}}-ring, but a {{sigma}}-ring need not be a {{sigma}}-field.

A {{sigma}}-ring <math>\mathcal{R}</math> that is a collection of subsets of <math>X</math> induces a [[Sigma-algebra|{{sigma}}-field]] for <math>X.</math> Define <math>\mathcal{A} = \{ E \subseteq X : E \in \mathcal{R} \ \text{or} \ E^c \in \mathcal{R} \}.</math> Then <math>\mathcal{A}</math> is a {{sigma}}-field over the set <math>X</math> - to check closure under countable union, recall a <math>\sigma</math>-ring is closed under countable intersections. In fact <math>\mathcal{A}</math> is the minimal {{sigma}}-field containing <math>\mathcal{R}</math> since it must be contained in every {{sigma}}-field containing <math>\mathcal{R}.</math>
